cheat_sheet.title: Security Mindset, Risk and the CIA Triad — Structural Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.introduction: This sheet turns Security Mindset, Risk and the CIA Triad into visible relationships. It is a reference for planning, tracing, debugging, and explaining—not a list to memorize.
cheat_sheet.why_it_matters: The level contributes directly to a defensive security improvement portfolio. Each concept helps the learner move from an ambiguous task to a contract, a representation, a verified transition, and an explainable result.

mental_model.summary: Represent the work as assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries before translating it into implementation details.
reasoning_cycle: Model variables, state, constraints, and relationships

input_questions: What may be absent or malformed?
output_questions: What shape and state are promised?

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.
debugging_checklist: Can I restate the exact expected output?
Are input shape, units, identity, and trust level explicit?
Which state is allowed to change?
Which invariant should hold after every step?
What is the first observed step that differs from the expected trace?
Is the boundary inclusive or exclusive?
Can an invalid or repeated event mutate valid state?
Are asynchronous or external results stale, missing, or out of order?
Does the representation match the operation mix and constraints?
Did the repair pass the original failure and nearby regression cases?

lessons.title: Assets, value, and security objectives
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Assets, value, and security objectives within the fictional Northstar Learning Lab.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Assets, value, and security objectives to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Assets, value, and security objectives is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Security begins by identifying what has value, who depends on it, and which confidentiality, integrity, and availability properties matter.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Assets, value, and security objectives, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Assets, value, and security objectives
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Security begins by identifying what has value, who depends on it, and which confidentiality, integrity, and availability properties matter.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Assets, value, and security objectives.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

Trace the transition and compare the result with the contract.

worked_examples.scenario: The input is exactly at the smallest or largest documented valid boundary.
worked_examples.input: A boundary value explicitly included by the constraint.
reasoning: Write the inclusive or exclusive boundary symbolically.
Evaluate the predicate before changing state.
Apply the same rule used for ordinary valid input.
Verify that the output remains representable and accessible.
worked_examples.output: The boundary case is accepted once and produces a valid output without special hidden state.

worked_examples.title: Rejected case: preserve the invariant
worked_examples.scenario: An input violates one required relationship or arrives in an unsupported state.
worked_examples.input: An out-of-contract value paired with a previously valid state.
reasoning: Identify the failed constraint and stop before commit.
Keep the previous valid state unchanged.
Return a specific, non-sensitive explanation or recovery path.
Record the case as evidence for a regression check.
worked_examples.output: A controlled rejection, preserved prior state, and actionable feedback.

structured_representation.caption: A validate-before-commit trace for Assets, value, and security objectives.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Assets, value, and security objectives' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.
progressive_hints: Label the input and promised output before naming any tool or syntax.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Threats, vulnerabilities, and controls is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A threat can exploit a vulnerability; a control prevents, detects, or helps recover from the resulting harm.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Threats, vulnerabilities, and controls, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Integrity decisions is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Integrity protects authorized and accurate change through validation, permissions, hashes, versioning, and audit evidence.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Integrity decisions, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Security trade-offs and defense in depth
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Security trade-offs and defense in depth within the fictional Northstar Learning Lab.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Security trade-offs and defense in depth to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Security trade-offs and defense in depth is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Layered controls reduce single points of failure while decisions balance risk reduction, usability, cost, and operational burden.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Security trade-offs and defense in depth, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Security trade-offs and defense in depth
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract

Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

project.title: Security Mindset, Risk and the CIA Triad: Defensive Security Improvement Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs the fictional Northstar Learning Lab that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate defensive security improvement portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Security Mindset, Risk and the CIA Triad. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Security begins by identifying what has value, who depends on it, and which confidentiality, integrity, and availability properties matter.
A threat can exploit a vulnerability; a control prevents, detects, or helps recover from the resulting harm.
Risk priority combines evidence about likelihood and impact instead of treating every weakness as equally urgent.
Confidentiality limits information disclosure through classification, least privilege, secure transport, and controlled sharing.
Integrity protects authorized and accurate change through validation, permissions, hashes, versioning, and audit evidence.
Availability uses redundancy, capacity, backups, monitoring, and recovery plans to keep required services usable.
A trust boundary marks where assumptions change; every exposed input or capability expands the attack surface that controls must cover.
Layered controls reduce single points of failure while decisions balance risk reduction, usability, cost, and operational burden.

constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.
Use only the fictional isolated lab and supplied fictional data.
No live target, public system, real account, harmful payload, persistence, evasion, credential capture, or destructive action is permitted.
Stop immediately when scope, ownership, monitoring, or impact is uncertain.

debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.

lessons.title: Accounts, processes, and least privilege
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Accounts, processes, and least privilege within the fictional Northstar Learning Lab.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Accounts, processes, and least privilege to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Accounts, processes, and least privilege is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Separate identities and grant each process only the resources required for its documented task.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Accounts, processes, and least privilege, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.body: Use assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Network layers and packet journeys, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Addressing, ports, and service exposure is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. An address locates a host and a port identifies a service endpoint; exposed listeners must match documented need.

Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Segmentation and firewall decisions
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Segmentation and firewall decisions within the fictional Northstar Learning Lab.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Segmentation and firewall decisions to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Segmentation and firewall decisions is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Segmentation limits paths between trust zones; firewall rules should allow explicit required flows and deny unnecessary reachability.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Segmentation and firewall decisions, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Segmentation and firewall decisions
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Segmentation limits paths between trust zones; firewall rules should allow explicit required flows and deny unnecessary reachability.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.

project.title: Operating-System, Network and Protocol Security: Defensive Security Improvement Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs the fictional Northstar Learning Lab that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate defensive security improvement portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Operating-System, Network and Protocol Security. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Separate identities and grant each process only the resources required for its documented task.
Ownership and access rules should start restrictive, be reviewed against need, and avoid unsafe convenience defaults.
Inventory systems, assess exposure and impact, test updates, deploy by priority, and verify remediation.
Data is encapsulated across layers and forwarded hop by hop; each boundary exposes different metadata and control points.
An address locates a host and a port identifies a service endpoint; exposed listeners must match documented need.
DNS maps names, while TLS authenticates endpoints and protects transport confidentiality and integrity when validation succeeds.
Segmentation limits paths between trust zones; firewall rules should allow explicit required flows and deny unnecessary reachability.

cheat_sheet.title: Web, Application and API Security — Structural Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.introduction: This sheet turns Web, Application and API Security into visible relationships. It is a reference for planning, tracing, debugging, and explaining—not a list to memorize.
cheat_sheet.why_it_matters: The level contributes directly to a defensive security improvement portfolio. Each concept helps the learner move from an ambiguous task to a contract, a representation, a verified transition, and an explainable result.

mental_model.summary: Represent the work as assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries before translating it into implementation details.
reasoning_cycle: Model variables, state, constraints, and relationships

output_questions: What shape and state are promised?

core_concepts.title: Application trust boundaries
core_concepts.rule: Map browser, API, database, third-party, and administrator boundaries so every untrusted transition has validation and authorization.

core_concepts.title: Input validation and output encoding
core_concepts.rule: Validate input for expected shape and encode output for its destination context; the two controls solve different boundary problems.

core_concepts.title: Authentication and session defense
core_concepts.rule: Strong identity proof, protected credentials, expiration, revocation, and anomaly detection reduce account and session risk.

core_concepts.title: Authorization and object-level access
core_concepts.rule: Every protected operation re-evaluates the actor, action, and target object on the server, regardless of interface visibility.

core_concepts.title: Secure API contracts and rate controls
core_concepts.rule: Strict schemas, bounded payloads, consistent errors, quotas, and monitoring limit misuse and accidental overload.

core_concepts.title: Browser-origin protections
core_concepts.rule: Origin policy, safe cookie attributes, CSRF defenses, and content restrictions reduce unintended cross-site actions and script execution.

core_concepts.title: Dependency and software-supply-chain risk
core_concepts.rule: Pin, verify, inventory, scan, minimize, and update dependencies through reviewed and reproducible build steps.

core_concepts.title: Threat modeling and remediation planning
core_concepts.rule: Prioritize feasible abuse paths, select layered controls, assign owners and deadlines, then verify risk reduction.

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

lessons.title: Application trust boundaries
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Application trust boundaries within the fictional Northstar Learning Lab.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Application trust boundaries to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Application trust boundaries is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Map browser, API, database, third-party, and administrator boundaries so every untrusted transition has validation and authorization.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Application trust boundaries, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Input validation and output encoding is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Validate input for expected shape and encode output for its destination context; the two controls solve different boundary problems.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Input validation and output encoding, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Authentication and session defense is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Strong identity proof, protected credentials, expiration, revocation, and anomaly detection reduce account and session risk.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Authentication and session defense, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Authorization and object-level access to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Authorization and object-level access is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Every protected operation re-evaluates the actor, action, and target object on the server, regardless of interface visibility.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Authorization and object-level access, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use assets, threats, vulnerabilities, controls, logs, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Authorization and object-level access
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Every protected operation re-evaluates the actor, action, and target object on the server, regardless of interface visibility.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Authorization and object-level access.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Authorization and object-level access' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.

project.title: Web, Application and API Security: Defensive Security Improvement Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs the fictional Northstar Learning Lab that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate defensive security improvement portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Web, Application and API Security. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Map browser, API, database, third-party, and administrator boundaries so every untrusted transition has validation and authorization.
Validate input for expected shape and encode output for its destination context; the two controls solve different boundary problems.
Strong identity proof, protected credentials, expiration, revocation, and anomaly detection reduce account and session risk.
Every protected operation re-evaluates the actor, action, and target object on the server, regardless of interface visibility.
Strict schemas, bounded payloads, consistent errors, quotas, and monitoring limit misuse and accidental overload.
Origin policy, safe cookie attributes, CSRF defenses, and content restrictions reduce unintended cross-site actions and script execution.
Pin, verify, inventory, scan, minimize, and update dependencies through reviewed and reproducible build steps.
Prioritize feasible abuse paths, select layered controls, assign owners and deadlines, then verify risk reduction.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Public-key encryption and signatures is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Public-key systems separate public and private operations; encryption protects secrecy while signatures provide origin and integrity evidence.

Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Key management and cryptographic agility is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Keys need generation, storage, access control, rotation, backup, revocation, and replacement plans independent of application code.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Key management and cryptographic agility, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract

project.title: Cryptography, Identity and Data Protection: Defensive Security Improvement Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs the fictional Northstar Learning Lab that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate defensive security improvement portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Cryptography, Identity and Data Protection. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Choose cryptography only after defining the confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, or non-repudiation property and the adversary's capability.
A cryptographic hash maps arbitrary input to a fixed digest with collision and preimage resistance; it does not hide data.
Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret, and modern authenticated modes require unique nonces under a key.
Public-key systems separate public and private operations; encryption protects secrecy while signatures provide origin and integrity evidence.
A certificate binds an identity to a public key, and validation checks chain, hostname, time, purpose, and revocation evidence.
Provisioning, authentication, recovery, role change, and deprovisioning form one identity lifecycle with high-risk transitions.
Classification determines handling, access, encryption, sharing, retention, and verified deletion requirements.
Keys need generation, storage, access control, rotation, backup, revocation, and replacement plans independent of application code.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Security telemetry and log quality is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Useful telemetry has synchronized time, stable identity, event outcome, source context, protected integrity, and bounded sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Security telemetry and log quality, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Triage and evidence preservation is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Triage establishes scope and urgency while recording provenance and preserving original evidence before deeper analysis.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Triage and evidence preservation, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Incident-response lifecycle is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and learning form an iterative response process.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Incident-response lifecycle, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Monitoring, Defensive Operations and Incident Response: Defensive Security Improvement Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs the fictional Northstar Learning Lab that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate defensive security improvement portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Monitoring, Defensive Operations and Incident Response. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Useful telemetry has synchronized time, stable identity, event outcome, source context, protected integrity, and bounded sensitive data.
A detection compares observable behavior to a rule or baseline; thresholds balance missed events against investigation cost.
Triage establishes scope and urgency while recording provenance and preserving original evidence before deeper analysis.
Preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and learning form an iterative response process.
Containment limits ongoing harm but must consider evidence, safety, service dependency, and the possibility of alerting an adversary.
Recovery restores trusted service in stages and verifies configuration, data integrity, monitoring, and recurrence controls.
Roles, severity, audience, cadence, known facts, uncertainty, and decisions keep technical and organizational response aligned.
A blameless review connects contributing conditions to owned corrective actions and measurable verification.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 5 supplies only constraints, acceptance criteria, and review checkpoints.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Security telemetry and log quality and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Baselines, detections, and false positives and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Triage and evidence preservation and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Incident-response lifecycle and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Containment and business trade-offs and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Recovery and validation and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Communication and decision records and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Post-incident learning and control improvement and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.
Use only the fictional isolated lab and supplied fictional data.
No live target, public system, real account, harmful payload, persistence, evasion, credential capture, or destructive action is permitted.
Stop immediately when scope, ownership, monitoring, or impact is uncertain.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

maximum documented size
duplicate or retry
out-of-order or stale result
malformed or unauthorized input
debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.
Name one design trade-off and the evidence behind your choice.
What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?

optional_mastery_challenge.title: Optional Mastery Transfer
optional_mastery_challenge.prompt: Transfer the level's eight governing rules to a new version of the fictional Northstar Learning Lab with one changed constraint, one new failure state, and one stricter evidence requirement.
required_outputs: change-impact table across all eight skills
normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery traces
success_criteria: The changed constraint is applied consistently.
No unaffected invariant is silently removed.
The new failure state has visible recovery behavior.
